clue.text: He got us lit up — but he had the liver trouble

definitions.meaning: the Titan of Greek myth who stole fire from the gods and gave it to mankind
as punishment the same Titan was chained to a rock while an eagle ate his liver daily

explanation.surface: Someone who got us drunk turns out to have suffered from a bad liver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lit up' suggests drunkenness, and liver trouble seems its consequence; both halves are Greek myth: the fire-bringer and his eagle.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves describe the same mythical Titan: giver of fire to humans, then punished by an eagle tearing at his liver.

clue.text: The pastry in the advertisement

definitions.meaning: flaky light pastry, as in a cream-filled bun
exaggerated praise used to promote something

explanation.surface: A pastry featured in an advert.
explanation.definitionFit: A light flaky pastry and an inflated promotional plug share one word.

clue.text: Everybody follows somebody

parts.note: the phrase meaning everyone is built from a word for a single person, then 'and', then a word for everybody following it

explanation.surface: A remark that all people are followers of someone.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase for everybody ends with ALL (everybody) after ONE (somebody) and 'and'.
explanation.definitionFit: The set phrase means every single person, all together.

clue.text: We think the world of our allotment

definitions.meaning: our planet
a rented garden plot, whose soil is what gardeners dig

explanation.surface: Gardeners say they adore their vegetable plot.
explanation.walkthrough: An allotment is a small plot of land rented for growing vegetables in Britain; its soil goes by the same name as our planet.
explanation.definitionFit: Our planet and garden soil share one name.

clue.text: Jog along, Leslie, though they rise in anger

parts.note: to hack is to ride a horse at an easy pace
Les is the short form of Leslie

explanation.surface: Telling Leslie to go jogging, even though tempers are rising.
explanation.walkthrough: HACK (ride at an ordinary pace) plus LES (short for Leslie).
explanation.definitionFit: Hackles are neck hairs that bristle when an animal is roused, hence the idiom of temper rising.

clue.text: Pan, you sound silent oddly enough

indicators.note: the word for the listener is said aloud and kept to one letter of the same sound

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced like you

indicators.note: something odd is out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Addressing the god Pan, remarking that he has gone strangely quiet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' turns 'you' into the letter U; 'oddly enough' rearranges SILENT into TENSIL. Pan is a kitchen pan, not the god.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucepan is one kind of kitchen implement.

clue.text: Whip up the yield

definitions.meaning: a riding whip is a short stick with a loop
the harvest gathered from a field

explanation.surface: An instruction to beat the harvest into shape.
explanation.definitionFit: A riding whip and a season's harvest share one short word.

clue.text: A horseman-what has he to prove ?

definitions.meaning: someone mounted on a horse
in geometry an extra proposition appended to a theorem, which the student must prove

explanation.surface: Asking what a horseman has to prove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'He' looks like the horseman again, but the second sense is a geometry exercise added to a theorem.
explanation.definitionFit: A mounted person; also an extra proposition, a supplementary problem set for proof.

clue.text: Where hot money originates for suckers ?

definitions.text: Where hot money originates for suckers ?

parts.words: Where hot money originates for suckers
parts.note: a spicy seasoning is hot, a coin factory is where money comes from, and the result is a sweet for sucking

explanation.surface: Asking where stolen money comes from for gullible victims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot money' looks like stolen cash and 'suckers' like dupes; really PEPPER (hot) plus MINT (where money originates) gives a sweet to suck.
explanation.definitionFit: A strongly flavoured sweet that people suck, made from a pungent herb.

clue.text: Enough to illuminate half the covered way

definitions.text: Enough to illuminate half the covered way

parts.words: Enough to illuminate half the covered way
parts.note: the first half of a word for a covered walkway, with lights enough to brighten it

explanation.surface: Lighting just sufficient for half a covered walk.
explanation.walkthrough: ARC is half of ARCADE (a covered way), and LAMPS are enough to illuminate it.
explanation.definitionFit: Powerful electric lights using an arc between electrodes, enough for lighting a large space.

clue.text: Mock at a fugitive

definitions.meaning: to jeer or sneer at someone
one who flees, read as a noun formed from the verb

explanation.surface: Someone jeering at a runaway.
explanation.definitionFit: To sneer is an old verb of this spelling; read as 'one who flees', the same letters name a runaway.

clue.text: Depression solved

parts.note: reads as a cure for low spirits, but a weather depression passing leaves the sky clear, and a solved mystery is also settled

explanation.surface: Someone's low mood has been cured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' is the weather system, not gloom: when it passes the sky clears, and the same phrase means a problem settled.
explanation.definitionFit: A solved problem has been sorted out, and a passing low-pressure system leaves fine weather, both expressed by one phrasal verb.

clue.text: Some stock-piles of industry are low

definitions.text: Some stock-piles of industry are low

parts.words: Some stock-piles of industry are low
parts.note: the industrious creatures are insects famed for hard work, and the heaps they build are small mounds

explanation.surface: A remark that factory stockpiles are running short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Industry' is the proverbial diligence of insects, and 'low' describes the small mounds rather than depleted stocks.
explanation.definitionFit: Insect colonies pile up earth into little hills, the heaps built by the creatures proverbial for industry.

clue.text: It's great to be free — at first

definitions.meaning: big, of considerable size
with 'at' placed first, the phrase means on the loose, as an escaped prisoner is

explanation.surface: A cheerful remark that freedom feels wonderful at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like 'initially' but is an instruction: put AT in front of the word, and the phrase means free.
explanation.definitionFit: Big is a plain synonym; an escaped convict 'at' this word is free.

clue.text: Pump or précis-writer

definitions.meaning: a machine that squeezes gas into a smaller volume
someone who squeezes a long text into a short summary

explanation.surface: Choosing between a pump and a summary writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that squeezes air and, read literally, one who squeezes text into a summary.

clue.text: Some rounds of Danes' bells

definitions.meaning: citrus fruits are round, so some of them are a few round things
in the London nursery rhyme the bells of St Clement Danes church ring out the name of this fruit and lemons

explanation.surface: A peal of bells rung by Danish ringers.
explanation.walkthrough: The held text dropped words; the scan gives them. St Clement Danes is a church on London's Strand whose bells, in the nursery rhyme, say 'Oranges and lemons'.
explanation.definitionFit: Round citrus fruits, and the fruit named by the church bells in the well-known London rhyme.

clue.text: Gunman's got old, mixed fifty drinks

parts.note: gat is an old form of the past tense got
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

indicators.note: mixed drinks are stirred together, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: gins are drinks

explanation.surface: A gunman grew old after mixing fifty drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mixed' shuffles fifty and drinks into LINGS. 'Got old' is the archaic past tense, not ageing; the Gatling gun is named after its inventor, so 'Gunman's' is possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: Hand-cranked machine guns named after their inventor, Richard Gatling.

clue.text: Cash equivalent of a nugget ?.

parts.note: a gold nugget is a lump of metal, and money paid all at once is the cash version of that

explanation.surface: Asking what a gold nugget is worth in money.
explanation.walkthrough: A nugget is a lump; a single payment in place of instalments is the cash 'lump'.
explanation.definitionFit: A single payment of the whole amount is a monetary lump, just as a nugget is a lump of gold.

clue.text: Lolly from the mountain sheep

definitions.meaning: British for a sweet
Peacock's verse says the mountain sheep are sweeter

explanation.surface: A sweet that came from a sheep on the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: A lolly is a sweet in Britain. Thomas Love Peacock's poem says 'The mountain sheep are sweeter', so they give sweet meat.
explanation.definitionFit: A sugary confection, and the sweeter flesh of hill sheep in Peacock's verse.

clue.text: Cloak of some drowned creature ?

parts.note: a drowned body is pallid, so drowned suggests pale
a tot is a small child, a little creature

explanation.surface: A garment belonging to some sea creature that has drowned.
explanation.walkthrough: PALE (a drowned person's colour) plus TOT (a small child) gives a loose overcoat's old name.
explanation.definitionFit: A paletot is a loose outer coat or cape, a kind of cloak.

clue.text: Bank has a way to avoid a row

definitions.text: Bank has a way to avoid a row

parts.words: Bank has a way to avoid a row
parts.note: the riverside track lets horses haul barges so nobody has to row them

explanation.surface: A bank has a method of escaping a quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like a quarrel and 'bank' like a lender: really a riverbank path where boats are hauled, not rowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A path along a canal or river bank used by horses hauling barges.

clue.text: Thus returns the bird, where the wheel is broken

indicators.note: the word for thus is turned to run the other way

parts.note: sic is Latin for thus
the tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A bird returns to a place where a wheel was smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' turns SIC into CIS. The definition quotes Ecclesiastes 12:6, 'or the wheel broken at the cistern'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible verse on death speaks of a wheel broken at the water tank, so the clue defines it by quotation.

clue.text: One of five' races, or just two

definitions.text: One of five' races, or just two

parts.words: One of five' races, or just two
parts.note: five famous English horse races carry this title, and the Greeks and Romans are the two ancient peoples whose works bear it

explanation.surface: Something counted among five races, or only two.
explanation.walkthrough: The five Classics are major English flat races (Derby, Oaks, St Leger, 2,000 and 1,000 Guineas); the two classical 'races' are the Greeks and Romans.
explanation.definitionFit: Five top horse races share this title, and the Greek and Roman peoples are called by its adjective.

clue.text: What disturbs an Asian nun I conclude is not excitement

parts.note: E for East, the direction of Asia

indicators.note: to disturb is to throw into disorder, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone concluding that a nun from Asia is troubled by tedium, not thrills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Disturbs' rearranges NUN I into NNUI, after E for Asian (East).
explanation.definitionFit: Listless boredom is the very opposite of excitement.

clue.text: Latest neckwear

parts.note: reads as fashionable collar wear, but means the last thing a hanged man wears round his neck

explanation.surface: The newest fashion in ties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Latest' suggests fashion, but it means last: the hangman's loop.
explanation.definitionFit: The hangman's looped rope is the final thing worn round a condemned neck.

clue.text: They display indescribably weird town hats

indicators.note: something weird is strange or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Peculiar hats worn in town are put on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Weird' rearranges TOWN HATS. The word means display shelves, and also things one cannot describe, which 'indescribably' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiered display stands are called by this name, which is also a term for indescribable odds and ends.

clue.text: Old sailor Peter, we hear makes it

definitions.text: Old sailor Peter, we hear makes it

parts.words: Old sailor Peter, we hear makes it
parts.note: an old sailor is a salt, and Peter said aloud gives petre: the two together name a substance that is this chemical

explanation.surface: An old seaman called Peter is said to succeed.
explanation.walkthrough: SALT (old sailor) plus PETRE (sounds like Peter) gives saltpetre, which is the chemical named.
explanation.definitionFit: Saltpetre, potassium nitrate, is the chemical also called by this short name.

clue.text: Show that went with a bang?

definitions.meaning: the 1960s rock musical of that title
a bang is a fringe

explanation.surface: A show that was a roaring success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went with a bang' suggests a hit; a bang is a straight-cut fringe.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous rock musical, and what a fringe or bang is cut from.

clue.text: Augustus, M.P.C. — the fellow's returned to his pasture in the Dell

indicators.note: the word for fellows comes back, read the other way

parts.note: dons are college fellows
a dell is a grassy hollow, and its pasture is grass

explanation.surface: A Club member named Augustus goes back to his field in a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returned' turns DONS into SNOD. Augustus Snodgrass is a Member of the Pickwick Club (M.P.C.) in Dickens's Pickwick Papers.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's poet character is a founding member of the Pickwick Club with the first name Augustus.

clue.text: The roofer from the attic?

parts.note: Attic is the Greek of Athens, and the letter it writes as a circle with a bar has the sound that begins the word for a straw roofer

explanation.surface: Someone who mends roofs emerging from a loft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Attic' is not a loft but Attic Greek; the roofer suggests a thatcher, whose opening sound that Greek letter stands for.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek letter of the Athenian alphabet, sounded th, as at the start of a straw roofer's trade name.

clue.text: Herb's sure wrong about foreign ways

indicators.note: letters set out wrongly are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Herb is sure he is mistaken about customs abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrong' rearranges SURE. 'Herb's' adds a second reading: rue is a herb, and 'rue's' sounds the same.
explanation.definitionFit: French streets are called by this word, so they are ways in a foreign country.

clue.text: Smart girl in the city

parts.note: chic means stylish or smart
Hester is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A fashionable young woman living in town.
explanation.walkthrough: Chichester is a cathedral city in West Sussex, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A cathedral city in southern England, county town of West Sussex.
